contents.text: What do you see when you picture a living thing? Often, people picture a large, macroscopic organism like a dog or a tree. But life can be extremely small, too! In fact, most life on Earth is microscopic. However, because microscopic things cannot be studied with the naked eye, they can be more difficult to identify as living or nonliving.
Read the passages to learn about Earth's microscopic bacteria and viruses.

pieces.text: are single-celled organisms. All bacteria have certain structures in common: a cell wall for structural support, a cell membrane to control the transport of nutrients and waste in and out of the cell, ribosomes to make proteins, and DNA containing genetic instructions the bacterium uses to grow and reproduce. The DNA and ribosomes are surrounded by a gel-like substance called cytoplasm. Some bacteria have specialized features, like protective outer capsules or whiplike tails called
Bacteria require a constant energy supply to grow, reproduce, and survive. Most bacteria are

Bacterial reproduction happens quickly—some species can double their population size every 20 minutes! So if a bacterium acquires a new, helpful genetic trait that helps it survive in its environment, it can very quickly pass on that trait until it spreads throughout the population.

are much smaller and simpler than bacteria. Viruses lack cell membranes, cytoplasm, and ribosomes—therefore, they are not considered cells. They also lack the machinery to process energy, grow, or even move on their own. Because of this, they do not eat or make food. Viruses typically store their genetic material—either DNA or RNA—inside a protective protein coat called a
, sometimes with a fatty outer envelope covered in proteins.

textContent.text: Inside its DNA or RNA are genetic instructions the virus needs to reproduce. But a virus can't reproduce on its own; it must take over a living cell. First, the virus drifts through the air, in liquids, or on surfaces until it bumps into and attaches to a host cell. It then injects its genetic material inside. The cell reads these instructions and is forced to stop its normal jobs to build new virus parts instead. Finally, these newly assembled viruses burst out of the cell, destroying it, and go on to infect other cells. A single virus can force a cell to create hundreds or thousands of new viruses at once! So if a virus acquires a new, helpful genetic trait that helps it survive in its environment, it can very quickly pass on that trait to many offspring.
